messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Environmental Scientist
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Arguments: Arguments, Affective Expression: Crying, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat

Vignette:
Tariq is a 19-year-old man of Jordanian descent who presents for an initial psychological evaluation accompanied by his wife, though he enters the consulting room ahead of her and immediately moves to the chair positioned with its back closest to the wall. He is soft-spoken and cooperative, though his eyes move steadily around the room during the intake, settling briefly on each face before returning to the door. He works as an environmental scientist for a municipal agency, a role he began just months after finishing an accelerated undergraduate program, and he describes his professional life with a quiet pride that sits in visible tension with the distress that has brought him here.

Tariq grew up in a household where his father's anger was the organizing fact of daily life. The abuse was not occasional or unpredictable in the way outsiders sometimes imagine; it was, in its own terrible way, structured. Arguments between his parents would build in a recognizable pattern — raised voices, the particular quality of silence that followed — and Tariq learned early to read the room with his whole body. What came next was often physical: a shove against a wall, a blow delivered from behind, the shock of contact he had not seen coming. He recalls with precision the sensation of being struck without warning, the way the unprepared body registers it differently from a blow one has braced for. He also remembers his mother crying in the kitchen afterward, a sound that to a young child signaled not comfort but the confirmation that something terrible had already happened or was still happening. He endured this from early childhood until he left for university at seventeen, and for a time the distance of the dormitory and the absorbing work of his studies seemed to place it behind him.

It was after his marriage, at eighteen, that the symptoms became impossible to ignore. Living again in close domestic proximity — the ordinary friction of two people sharing a small apartment, the occasional disagreements that any young couple navigates — something shifted. When he and his wife argued, even mildly, Tariq found himself flooded with a physical urgency he could not explain to her. His chest would tighten, his vision would narrow, and he would feel with absolute certainty that the argument was about to become something much worse. He had come to believe, in a way that felt less like a thought and more like a fact embedded in his body, that raised voices meant that harm was imminent. Similarly, when his wife or a colleague became visibly upset and cried, Tariq would feel a cold dread settle over him — not sympathy, but alarm, the sense of standing in that kitchen again. And if someone touched him without his seeing it coming — a hand on his shoulder from a coworker, a colleague brushing past him in the corridor of the agency's field office — he would flinch violently and sometimes step away before he had consciously registered what had happened.

Over the months since the marriage, Tariq has arranged his life around the management of these responses in ways that have begun to cost him concretely. At the office, he positions himself at the end of the table in every meeting, back to the partition wall, and he has turned down two invitations to participate in fieldwork that would have required sharing vehicles and close quarters with colleagues he does not know well. He has developed a habit of arriving early to any room so that he can choose where to sit before others enter. He scans the faces of coworkers and strangers with an attention that he knows is excessive — searching for the particular tightening around the jaw, the shift in posture — because he was certain that if he could detect the warning signs early enough, he would not be caught unprepared the way he had been as a child. He avoids being in the office alone after hours, and he has also begun declining social invitations, finding the management of unfamiliar people's expressions and movements exhausting in a way he struggles to articulate. His wife has noticed the withdrawal, and it is her gentle insistence, more than anything else, that has brought him here.

What Tariq is most afraid of, he says quietly at the end of the intake, is that there is something permanently wrong with him — that the vigilance is simply who he is now. What he hopes for, with a carefulness that suggests he does not entirely trust the hope, is that it does not have to be.
